source.title: Code Llama: Open Foundation Models for Code
source.authors: Baptiste Rozière; Jonas Gehring; Fabian Gloeckle; Sten Sootla; Itai Gat; Xiaoqing Tan; Yossi Adi; Jingyu Liu; Romain Sauvestre; Tal Remez; J. Rapin; Artyom Kozhevnikov; I. Evtimov; Joanna Bitton; Manish P Bhatt; Cristian Canton Ferrer; Aaron Grattafiori; Wenhan Xiong; Alexandre Défossez; Jade Copet; Faisal Azhar; Hugo Touvron; Louis Martin; Nicolas Usunier; Thomas Scialom; Gabriel Synnaeve

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream coding benchmark scores across model sizes, testing a downstream-scaling version of the claim, but it does not fit or test the original held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The reported pass@1 scaling results for Code Llama and Code Llama - Python are recorded below. The paper also shows training-perplexity curves, but these are training rather than held-out losses and do not test V1; they are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited Chinchilla scaling-law findings are not study results and are excluded.
record.test_reason: A model-release paper, not a scaling study. Its own Table 2 compares downstream pass@1 across 7B–70B code-specialized models trained by the same process, which bears weakly on V6 in a new setting (code fine-tunes of Llama 2). It fits no curve, makes no prediction from loss and has no held-out loss sweep, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say larger code-specialized models outperform smaller ones on almost every HumanEval/MBPP/APPS metric. They hypothesize further gains from scaling and cite Chinchilla that larger models would benefit from more tokens. They fit no scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Uses code-specialized Code Llama model families and downstream pass@1 benchmarks across sizes, rather than held-out pretraining loss scaling or power-law fitting. Training data, initialization, and specialization differ from the original scaling-law measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream score levels vary by model specialization (Code Llama versus Code Llama - Python); the paper also reports that infilling, long-context fine-tuning, and instruction fine-tuning affect coding benchmark outcomes. For the recorded scaling scores, HumanEval is zero-shot and MBPP is 3-shot.

fits_no_version.finding: Training perplexity keeps decreasing through 500B code tokens for 7B/13B/34B. A scratch-trained 7B reaches Code Llama 7B's training loss only at about half its training (240B fewer tokens).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initializing from a general pretrained model shifts the code-training loss trajectory. These are training-loss observations, not held-out scaling laws.

record.problems: The scaling results are downstream benchmark scores, not held-out pretraining losses; no power-law fits, extrapolation tests, or uncertainty estimates for the benchmark scores are reported. Training-perplexity evidence appears as curves rather than a held-out loss evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: No other downstream size-sweep scores were extracted; this record includes HumanEval and MBPP pass@1 for the two families with clearly attributable values in Table 2. Other benchmark results and variants were not needed to establish the tested V6 trend.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fitted trend, no extrapolation to larger models and no downstream-versus-pretraining-loss relation. Only 4 sizes, with token count changing at 70B.
No held-out pretraining loss sweep or power-law fit.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No loss scaling-law fit for code fine-tuning.

missing.what: Code Llama - Instruct pass@1 by size on HumanEval/MBPP, including the non-monotone 13B→34B HumanEval step (42.7%→41.5%).
Code Llama - Instruct APPS zero-shot by size; introductory pass@5 decreases with size.
MultiPL-E pass@1 by size and language. This includes a non-monotone Code Llama - Python 13B→34B average (39.6%→36.8% without LCFT), plus the authors' remark that the 34B Python variant underperforms.
Two further size series: APPS two-shot by size for base/Python (Table 3) and GSM8K solve rate by size (Table 12; 13.0→20.8→32.7% for Code Llama).

record.verdict_notes: Weak, incidental evidence. There are only four sizes, fine-tuned from Llama 2 base models that were themselves of different scale. 70B saw twice the code tokens, and 34B lacks FIM. The reader's T2 is changed to T3 because this is a new setting (code specialization) with no method aimed at the scaling question. Figure 4a validation perplexity varies context length, not scale, and bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute; the reported loss curves are training perplexity.
No prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
No fixed-compute comparison of parameter/token allocations or fitted compute-optimal trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of the same loss scaling form across modalities or the listed other training regimes.
Tests downstream code-generation benchmark scores across model sizes, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss, a fitted predictive relationship, or non-code tasks.
No analysis of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation sensitivity to counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Base Code Llama and Code Llama - Python, HumanEval (0-shot) and MBPP (3-shot) pass@1, greedy decoding, 7B–70B
relationships.reason: pass@1 rises monotonically with size in all four series (e.g. MBPP 41.4→47.0→55.0→62.4); rows r1–r16. The trend is monotone only and no predictive fit is given.
relationships.display_finding: pass@1 increased monotonically in all four series, including MBPP scores of 41.4, 47.0, 55.0, and 62.4, without a predictive fit.

relationships.condition: Instruction-tuned variants, some MultiPL-E languages and some pass@100 settings (from text; no rows)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows. Scaling is non-monotone in places: Instruct HumanEval pass@1 13B 42.7% vs 34B 41.5% (Table 2), and Instruct APPS zero-shot introductory pass@5 drops 24.9% (7B)→19.8% (34B) (Table 15). Code Llama - Python MultiPL-E average falls 39.6% (13B)→36.8% (34B) (Table 11), and Code Llama MBPP pass@100 falls 87.1% (13B)→86.6% (34B).
relationships.display_finding: Instruct HumanEval pass@1 fell from 42.7% to 41.5%, Instruct APPS introductory pass@5 from 24.9% to 19.8%, Python MultiPL-E average from 39.6% to 36.8%, and MBPP pass@100 from 87.1% to 86.6%.
